extraction.name: Common Corpus
extraction.description: The largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing about two trillion tokens from uncopyrighted or permissively licensed sources across multiple languages and including collections for Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Code, Open Web, and Open Semantic.
extraction.creator: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov
extraction.citeAs: Langlais, Pierre-Carl et al. Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training. arXiv:2506.01732v1, 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus has been an ongoing effort since 2024 and was assembled from six collections: Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic. Data were aggregated from public domain and permissively licensed sources, including collection-as-data initiatives, APIs, official open data portals, OpenAlex, Wikimedia projects, YouTube transcripts, StackExchange, The Stack v1 and v2, and Wikidata adapted into natural language through a collaboration with Wikimedia Deutschland. Open Culture was compiled from Collections As Data dumps and resource-by-resource retrieval using APIs and other standard retrieval methods whenever available. The dataset is available on HuggingFace as an aggregation of 10,000 parquet files.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Web Scraping, Web API, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include public domain and permissively licensed documents from government, legal, financial, cultural heritage, scientific, code, web, and semantic data sources. Examples explicitly named include SEC annual reports from EDGAR, WTO Documents Online, AMF documents, TED EU tenders, GATT Library, Europarl, Caselaw Access Project, CourtListener, EUR-Lex, Eurovoc/Cellar, French administrative open data, USPTO, UN Digital Library, OECD, Gallica, Chronicling America, Europeana, Biblioteca Digital Hispánica, Delpher, Papers Past, OpenAlex-linked PDFs, arXiv articles, Stack v1 and v2 from GitHub, Wikimedia projects, YouTube transcripts, StackExchange, and Wikidata RDF triples converted to natural language.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The Common Corpus effort has been ongoing since 2024. Source documents span wide historical periods depending on collection, including examples such as GATT documents from 1946 to 1996, WTO documents from 1995 to 2024, SEC reports from 1993 to 2024, AMF and other modern administrative data, and cultural heritage materials from as early as the 17th century through the 20th century.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data were filtered and curated for licensing, quality, and safety. For Open Science, OpenAlex was filtered to CC-By, Public Domain/CC0, and CC-By-SA licenses. For Open Code, files outside desired languages and formats were removed by file extension; non-informative file types and files with 75% or more digits were removed; licenses were filtered to keep only permissible ones; and manual filters from Lozhkov et al. (2024) were applied. For Open Semantic, Wikidata RDF triples were transformed into formal natural language sequences, and all available translations for an entry were provided as consecutive blocks separated by a newline. For Open Culture, an internal rights verification process was applied when institutional guarantees were insufficient, using criteria such as author life and object creation time and restricting collection to institutions based in the US or EU.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing included text segmentation with Segmentext; OCR quality assessment with OCRoscope and OCRerrcr; OCR correction with OCRonos for OCR errors, wrong word cuts or merges, and broken text structures; PII detection and replacement using Microsoft's Presidio with custom regular expressions for phone numbers; and toxicity filtering of public domain training data using the multilingual classifier Celadon. The paper also states that they remove personally identifiable information, engage in extensive OCR correction and toxicity filtering for public domain datasets, and for Open Code replaced sequences of [\r]+\n with \n and recalculated line lengths before filtering.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The paper does not describe human annotation for Common Corpus itself, but it does describe a separate multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon, trained from scratch on 2M annotated samples. Celadon identifies toxic and harmful content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse. This classifier was then used in the Common Corpus toxicity filtering pipeline to identify documents containing harmful language and either remove them or synthetically rewrite them without the harmful language.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Microsoft's Presidio, Celadon, fastText language identification model, cld2
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus was first published in March 2024, became a unified corpus in November 2024, and the version described in the paper was released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit. The paper states that Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset, with HuggingFace ensuring proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally identifiable information (PII), including examples such as phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses, is discussed as sensitive data. The dataset creators state that they remove personally identifiable information from their datasets and replace detected PII with fictitious but realistic values.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper frames Common Corpus as critical infrastructure for open science research in LLMs and argues that it enables open LLM research and development while meeting legal and regulatory requirements, including in the EU. It is presented as supporting fully open and auditable LLMs, contributing to the AI Commons, fostering reproducibility, and enabling multilingual and creative-writing-capable models without violating copyright law. The authors also state that they aim to inspire further responsible data collection initiatives.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly discusses that web data is a major source of harmful and biased content and cites sexual content, hate speech, and racial and gender biases in Common Crawl. It also notes that historical public domain texts in Open Culture may contain outdated and harmful language about ethnic groups, women, violence, and other themes that do not meet modern ethical standards. The authors state that training on such texts would reproduce and circulate harmful language, and they mitigate this through toxicity detection, removal, or synthetic rewriting.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper states that Common Corpus is far from collecting the whole range of available open data, calling this the open data paradox. Coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow. The total size of 2 trillion tokens is suitable for pre-training models of limited size, but larger models require significantly more data. Common Corpus does not contain data for instruction-tuning or specialized tasks and is therefore not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning. The curation methods, including toxicity detection and PII removal, do not achieve 100% accuracy. The paper also notes challenges such as poor OCR quality, text segmentation issues, irrecoverable deterioration of original supports, and unresolved license identification issues for permissively licensed web archives.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended primarily for language model pre-training and can be used on its own or in conjunction with existing open datasets. The paper also states it has been used to create multimodal datasets, classifiers, synthetic datasets, benchmarks, vision-language models for document segmentation and processing, historical language models, creative-writing-capable models, retrieval-augmented generation models, and speech/multimodal datasets derived from YouTube Commons. It is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning because it does not contain instruction-tuning or specialized task data.
